# Block 2: Inline completions {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Inline completion is the most familiar AI coding feature, and the simplest kind
of `r glossary("assistant")`: grey "ghost text" appears as you type,
suggesting a continuation. You accept with Tab, reject with
Esc, or ignore it by carrying on typing. This block teaches what context inline
completion uses, and the practical consequence: what you write immediately
before the cursor matters more than anything else.

Claude Code does not offer inline completion, so this is the one block where
GitHub Copilot is the main tool.

*⏱ ~25 minutes*


## Setup

You signed in to GitHub Copilot in the pre-work
([Setting up Claude Code](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd), Step 6). Use **one**
completion provider at a time during this block, so you know which tool
produced each suggestion.

Check it still works: open a blank R script and type
`# Calculate the mean of 1 to 100`. Within a second or two you should see
ghost text such as `mean(1:100)`. If nothing appears, press Enter to move to the
next line and wait.

**If no ghost text appears,** follow the instructor's screen for this block and
fix the set-up at the break, rather than losing the block to it. The set-up
routes, if you skipped the pre-work:

- **RStudio:** enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio's options and sign in to
  GitHub.
- **Positron:** see Positron's completions documentation for how to choose
  GitHub Copilot as the provider.
- **VS Code:** Copilot's AI features are built in. Select **Use AI Features**
  from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub.

Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the
time of writing); paid Copilot plans do not meter completions. Completions send
the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in
[Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd) apply here too.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

In RStudio and Positron you can use Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions instead of
Copilot. In RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button; it
requires a Posit AI account. In Positron, choose it as the completions
provider. Posit AI does not meter completions.
:::


## The context principle

A suggestion can only use what is in the model's
`r glossary("context window")` when it is made. GitHub Copilot fills that
window mainly from the current file: the code above and below the cursor, and
especially the comment immediately before it. In Positron and VS
Code it may also draw on other open tabs. It does not see your R session.

The practical consequence: the comment immediately before your cursor, and the
code above it, have the largest effect on what you get.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions also sees your live R session: the columns of
loaded data frames, functions you have defined and packages you have loaded.
A session-aware provider therefore adds one more lever: what you have loaded.
:::


## Activity: The context demonstration

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
The context demonstration (10 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** your workshop project is open, and inline completion produced
ghost text in the set-up check.

You will use `voles_metabolism.csv`, a small synthetic dataset chosen because
its column names are unlikely to appear in any model's training data. The
columns are `subject_id`, `sex`, `treatment_arm`, `mass_pre_g`, `mass_post_g`
and `metabolic_rate_post`. The data record a hypothetical metabolism trial in
72 voles, with three treatment arms and two sexes.

**1. No context.** Restart R, so that you are in a
`r glossary("fresh R session")` with nothing loaded. Open a blank R script.

**In the R script:** type only this comment, and wait.


```{r}
#| eval: false
# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment
```

Record the suggestion. With no `library()` call, no data and no column names
visible, the model has to guess. Expect something syntactically plausible but
wrong for this dataset.

**2. Context in the file.** Start a new blank script.

**In the R script:**


```{r}
#| eval: false
# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)
```

Then add the same comment as before on a new line.

**In the R script:**


```{r}
#| eval: false
# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment
```

Record the suggestion. A typical good result:

`r hide("Solution")`

```{r, eval = FALSE}
voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )
```

`r unhide()`

The exact form varies between people and sessions; that variation is itself
part of the lesson.

How different were the two outputs? Did the second use column names that exist
in the data? Did the model compute the change in the right direction (post
minus pre)?

**You are done when** you have recorded both suggestions and can say what the
second one had that the first did not.

**If it goes wrong:** if a suggestion never appears, type the comment again on a
new line; if your script stops running, *Session → Restart R* and run it from
the top.

::::
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

**3. Context in the session.** With Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, run the
lines from step 2 so that `voles` exists in your session. Then open a **new,
blank** script, type only the comment from step 1, and wait. If the suggestion
now uses the real column names, it came from your session, not from the file.
:::


## Activity: Build a small analysis

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Build a small analysis (10 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** the script from step 2 of the context demonstration, with
`voles` loaded.

In that script, drive inline completion through two analysis steps.
Write the comment for each step first, then accept, reject or modify the
suggestion.

**1. Summary table.** Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of
`mass_change_g` by `treatment_arm` and `sex`, with the number of observations
per cell. (Create `mass_change_g` first if your script does not have it.)

**2. Plot.** Produce one plot relating `mass_change_g` to `metabolic_rate_post`,
coloured by `treatment_arm`.

For each step, record the comment you wrote, the suggested code, and one line
saying whether you accepted, modified or rejected it. The point of the record is
to make you notice when you accepted something without inspecting it.

**You are done when** a fresh R session (*Session → Restart R*, then run the
script from the top) produces the summary table and one plot without error.

**If it goes wrong:** delete the last suggestion you accepted, and write a more
specific comment naming the data frame and its columns.

`r hide("An example")`

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

voles <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    subject_id = col_character(),
    sex = col_character(),
    treatment_arm = col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = col_double(),
    mass_post_g = col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = col_double()
  )
) |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g)

# mean and SD of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with n per cell
voles |>
  summarise(
    mean_change_g = mean(mass_change_g),
    sd_change_g = sd(mass_change_g),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)
  ) |>
  arrange(treatment_arm, sex)

# mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm
ggplot(voles, aes(metabolic_rate_post, mass_change_g, colour = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Metabolic rate (post-treatment)", y = "Change in mass (g)")
```

The plot drops the one animal with no metabolic rate and says so in a warning:
read the warning rather than ignore it.

`r unhide()`

::::
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** steer inline completion with a specific comment and the
  right code above the cursor, **trusted because** you decided on every
  suggestion and the script runs from a fresh R session.
- **Check:** accept, modify or reject every suggestion deliberately; your
  record of each decision is what makes you notice an unexamined acceptance.
- **Reproduce:** a suggestion that names your columns correctly came from
  context in the file or session, so the same comment in a blank script will
  not reproduce it.
- **Record:** nothing to log yet; your `r glossary("AI-use log")` starts in
  [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd), once an
  `r glossary("agent")` starts doing work.
:::


## Check your understanding

**The single most reliable way to improve inline suggestions in a new script
is to:**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Switch to a different underlying model",
  "Open more files in the editor as additional context",
  answer = "Write a specific comment immediately before the code you want, naming the data frame and its columns",
  "Restart the IDE so the assistant has a fresh context"
))`

**You get correct column names in a blank script using Posit AI Next Edit
Suggestions, but not with Copilot. The most likely reason is:**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Posit AI uses a larger model",
  answer = "Next Edit Suggestions can see the data frame loaded in your R session; Copilot sees only the files",
  "Copilot cannot read R code",
  "The column names were in Posit AI's training data"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

### The full four-step analysis

The live activity uses two of four steps. The full sequence, again writing the
comment for each step before accepting, rejecting or modifying the suggestion:

1. Filter to subjects with non-missing `metabolic_rate_post` and create a
   derived variable `mass_change_g`.
2. Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of
   `mass_change_g` by `treatment_arm` and `sex`, with the number of
   observations per cell.
3. Fit a linear model of `metabolic_rate_post` on `treatment_arm` and `sex`.
   Inspect the coefficients.
4. Produce one plot relating `mass_change_g` to `metabolic_rate_post`,
   coloured by `treatment_arm`.

When you have finished steps 2 and 4, post the code Copilot suggested for
step 4 in the Zoom chat, with a note on whether you accepted, changed or
rejected it. Then compare with what others posted: the comparison usually shows
different suggestions, different acceptance decisions and, often, different bugs.
